nameStory: The black-tailed red sheetweaver gets its colorful name from its striking two-toned appearance - a bright red or reddish body contrasted with a distinctive black abdomen tip that looks like it was dipped in ink. The 'sheetweaver' part refers to its web-building style, creating flat, sheet-like webs rather than the classic orb webs we often picture spiders making.
description: This tiny spider is a real eye-catcher despite its small size, typically measuring just a few millimeters across. The black-tailed red sheetweaver sports a vibrant red or orange-red body with a characteristic black marking on the rear of its abdomen that gives it its name. As a member of the dwarf spider family, it's quite small but makes up for its size with its distinctive coloring and interesting sheet-web hunting strategy. This is the only species in its genus, making it a unique find in New England.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive black 'tail' marking on the tip of an otherwise bright red or orange-red abdomen - this contrast is unmistakable and feels like nature's version of a warning flag

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small even for spiders, roughly the size of a pinhead or small bead - you'll need to look closely or use a magnifying glass to appreciate its beautiful coloring

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates flat, sheet-like webs close to the ground that feel delicate and filmy to the touch, often spanning between grass stems or low vegetation

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen that appears almost balloon-like, with a smaller reddish cephalothorax (front section) that has a smooth, glossy appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found walking on or near their sheet webs in grassy areas during the day, moving with quick, jerky motions when disturbed

habitat: In New England, look for black-tailed red sheetweaver in open, grassy areas like meadows, field edges, and well-maintained lawns where they can string their sheet webs between grass stems. They prefer sunny, open habitats with short to medium-height vegetation rather than dense forests or shaded areas. You might also spot them in agricultural areas, parks, and even suburban lawns with diverse plant growth.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to establish territories and build their characteristic sheet webs in emerging grass and early vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily spotted on their webs during warm, sunny days. This is the best time for identification as their bright coloring is most vivid.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, though they become less conspicuous as vegetation dies back and temperatures drop. Mating and egg-laying typically occur during this period.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures, but eggs overwinter in protected locations, waiting to hatch when spring returns.

funFact: Despite being called a 'red grass spider,' this tiny arachnid is actually more closely related to money spiders - those tiny spiders that supposedly bring good luck when they land on you - than to the large grass spiders that build funnel webs in lawns!
confusionNotes: The biggest confusion comes from its small size making it hard to spot, but once you see the red body with black tail combination, it's unmistakable. Other small red spiders in the area lack this distinctive black 'dipped in ink' appearance on their rear end.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'red grass spider' in some regions, this species belongs to an entirely different family than the large funnel-web grass spiders most people know. The common name can be misleading since it's actually a dwarf spider that builds sheet webs rather than funnel webs.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Florinda, the black-tailed red sheetweaver is unique among New England spiders. When comparing to other dwarf spiders in the sheetweb family, most are much duller in color - typically brown, gray, or black - making this species' bright red coloration with black tail marking absolutely distinctive. No other small spider in the region combines this vivid red and black color pattern.
